title: Playing with Numbers
prerequisites: Comfort with place value of digits in a multi-digit number.
Basic linear equation and algebraic manipulation skills from Chapter 2.
Familiarity with divisibility rules (for 2, 3, 5, 9, 10) from earlier classes.

topics.title: Numbers in General Form & Reversing Digits
topics.quick_summary: Any two- or three-digit number can be written algebraically in terms of its digits' place values, which allows number puzzles about digit reversal and digit sums to be solved using algebra.

detailed.definition: A two-digit number with tens digit 'a' and units digit 'b' is written in general form as 10a + b; a three-digit number with digits a (hundreds), b (tens), c (units) is written as 100a + 10b + c.
detailed.key_idea: Writing numbers in general (place-value) form converts a numerical pattern or puzzle into an algebraic expression that can be manipulated, factorised, or tested for divisibility just like any other algebraic expression.
detailed.working_principle: Represent the unknown number(s) using place-value notation with variables for each digit, translate the puzzle's conditions (like 'reverse the digits' or 'sum of digits') into algebraic expressions, then simplify or solve using standard algebraic techniques.
applications: Solving classic number puzzles and logical brain-teasers involving digit manipulation.
Proving general divisibility results (e.g., why the difference between a 2-digit number and its reverse is always divisible by 9).

topics.real_life: Verifying why a two-digit number is always divisible by 9 when added to its digit-reversed version and then divided by 11 (or similar classic number tricks) becomes provable using this general algebraic form.
points: Two-digit number with digits a, b: general form = 10a + b (a = tens digit, b = units digit).
Sum of a 2-digit number and its reverse: (10a+b) + (10b+a) = 11(a+b), always divisible by 11.
Difference of a 2-digit number and its reverse: (10a+b) − (10b+a) = 9(a−b), always divisible by 9.
mistakes: Writing the general form with digits in the wrong place-value position (e.g., writing ab instead of 10a+b).
Forgetting that digit values must be single digits (0 to 9), which constrains possible values of a, b, c in puzzle solutions.
Losing track of which digit is being called 'a' vs 'b' partway through a multi-step puzzle.
topics.memory_hook: 'Digits become variables' — 10a+b turns a number puzzle into an ordinary algebra problem.
topics.advanced: The results '(number) + (its reverse) is divisible by 11' and '(number) − (its reverse) is divisible by 9' are not coincidences — they fall directly out of the algebraic identity 11(a+b) and 9(a−b), showing how a seemingly 'magical' number trick is really just a disguised piece of straightforward algebra.

topics.title: Letters for Digits — Solving Number Puzzles & Divisibility Tests
topics.quick_summary: Cryptarithm-style puzzles use letters to represent unknown digits in an arithmetic sum, solved through logical deduction combined with divisibility rules for 2, 3, 5, 9, and 10.

detailed.definition: A 'letters for digits' puzzle replaces the digits of a sum with letters (each letter representing one fixed, unknown digit consistently); divisibility rules provide quick tests for whether a number (possibly containing an unknown digit) is divisible by a small number like 2, 3, 5, 9, or 10.
detailed.key_idea: In any letters-for-digits puzzle, each distinct letter represents ONE specific digit throughout the entire puzzle (never changing), and typically the leading digit of any number cannot be 0.
detailed.working_principle: Use column-by-column addition/subtraction logic starting from the units column, applying carry-over rules, and use process-of-elimination with the constraint that each letter is a single fixed digit (0–9) and leading digits are non-zero, to narrow down the unique solution.
applications: Recreational mathematics and logical reasoning puzzles that build systematic deduction skills.
Quick mental divisibility checks (e.g., checking if a large number is divisible by 9 by adding its digits) used throughout arithmetic and number theory.

topics.real_life: Classic puzzles like 'ON + ON = TOO' or determining the digit that makes a number divisible by 9, both rely on the systematic logic taught in this topic.
points: Divisibility by 2: last digit is even (0,2,4,6,8). Divisibility by 5: last digit is 0 or 5. Divisibility by 10: last digit is 0.
Divisibility by 3: sum of all digits is divisible by 3. Divisibility by 9: sum of all digits is divisible by 9.
In letters-for-digits puzzles, the SAME letter always represents the SAME digit everywhere it appears.
The leading (first) digit of any multi-digit number in the puzzle can never be 0.
mistakes: Allowing the same letter to take different digit values in different parts of the puzzle — this breaks the rules of the puzzle.
Forgetting to check that a leading digit isn't 0, which can eliminate otherwise 'valid-looking' solutions.
Confusing the divisibility rule for 3 (digit sum divisible by 3) with the rule for 9 (digit sum divisible by 9) — they use the same method but different divisors.
topics.memory_hook: 'Same letter, same digit, always' — and no number ever starts with a leading zero.
topics.advanced: Divisibility rules for 3 and 9 both work because 10 ≡ 1 (mod 3) and 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9) — every place value power of 10 leaves the same remainder of 1 when divided by 3 or 9, which is exactly why simply summing the digits (ignoring their place value) still correctly tests divisibility, a neat early glimpse into modular arithmetic explored formally in higher classes.
